concepts.title: Motion Field for Rotation Around Optical Axis
aliases: rotation around optical axis motion field
concepts.one_liner: The motion field for rotation along the camera optical axis ($W_X=W_Y=0$) is given by $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y \\ -x \end{bmatrix} W_Z$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the motion field for rotation around the optical axis helps describe how image points move when the camera rotates about its viewing direction, a fundamental case in motion analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rotation about the optical axis has $W_X=W_Y=0$.
- Motion field is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} y \\ -x \end{bmatrix} W_Z$.
- This describes the 2D image velocity induced by such rotation.

slots.motivation: Understanding the motion field for rotation around the optical axis helps describe how image points move when the camera rotates about its viewing direction, a fundamental case in motion analysis.

concepts.title: Motion Field for Rotation Around Y Axis
aliases: rotation around y axis motion field
concepts.one_liner: For rotation around the $y$-axis with $W_Z=0$ and $W_X=0$, the motion field is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} f^2+x^2 \\ xy \end{bmatrix} W_Y$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula characterizes the image motion induced by camera rotation around the $y$-axis, important for understanding how 3D rotations affect 2D image flow.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rotation around $y$-axis with $W_Z=0$, $W_X=0$ considered.
- Motion field: $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{f} \begin{bmatrix} f^2+x^2 \\ xy \end{bmatrix} W_Y$.
- Describes 2D image velocities from such rotation.

slots.motivation: This formula characterizes the image motion induced by camera rotation around the $y$-axis, important for understanding how 3D rotations affect 2D image flow.

concepts.title: Homography for Large Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: For large camera rotations, the relationship between images at times $t$ and $t+\Delta t$ is a homography.
concepts.content: In the case of camera rotation, for a large angle (or a large $\Delta t$), the relationship between the image at time $t$ and the image at time $t+\Delta t$ is a homography.
concepts.motivation_md: Large rotations cause complex image transformations that can be modeled as homographies, enabling accurate image alignment and motion understanding.
concepts.recap_md:
- Large camera rotations relate images via a homography.
- Applies for large rotation angles or large time intervals $\Delta t$.
- Homography captures the planar projective transformation between views.

concepts.title: Motion under Varying Focal Length
concepts.one_liner: Changing focal length produces a scaling motion field on the image plane without parallax, resulting in zoom and crop effects.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how varying focal length causes apparent image motion (zoom) without actual scene motion or parallax, clarifying a key source of image motion unrelated to 3D structure.
concepts.recap_md:
- Changing focal length produces a scaling motion field on the image plane.
- No parallax or depth information arises from focal length changes.
- Results in zoom and crop effects without scene motion.

motivation.text: As the sensor has finite size, changing the focal length results in a zoom and a crop. The motion field does not depend on the 3D scene structure. Therefore, images taken by a pinhole camera from the same viewpoint but with different focal lengths do not provide depth information about the scene.

concepts.title: Projection of 3D Point Motion into Image Plane
concepts.one_liner: A 3D point's trajectory projects into the image plane with a 2D instantaneous velocity derived from its 3D velocity.
concepts.content: A 3D point will follow a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$, in camera coordinates (@fig-optical_flow_basic_motion_point). As the point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The projection of this point into the image plane location is $\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$,
concepts.motivation_md: Relating 3D point motion to its 2D image projection is crucial for understanding optical flow and motion estimation.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 3D point moves along a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t)$.
- Its instantaneous 3D velocity is $\dot{\mathbf{P}}$.
- The 2D projection moves with instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}}$.

concepts.title: Perspective Projection Equations for Motion
concepts.one_liner: The instantaneous velocity in the image plane relates to 3D point motion via perspective projection equations involving focal length and depth.
concepts.motivation_md: These equations connect 3D motion to 2D image velocities, essential for understanding optical flow and motion estimation in images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perspective projection relates 3D points to 2D image points via $x=fX/Z$, $y=fY/Z$.
- Instantaneous image velocity depends on 3D velocity and depth $Z$.
- Matrix form expresses image velocity as a function of 3D velocity and camera parameters.

key_passage.text: Using the equations of perspective projection $x=f X/Z$ and $y=f Y/Z$ (assuming that the camera is at the origin of the world-coordinate system), we can derive the equations of how the instantaneous velocity in the camera plane relates to the point motion in 3D world coordinates: $$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\ \dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} \end{aligned}$$ The second expression is obtained by using $x=f \, X/Z$ and $y=f \, Y/Z$, which removes the dependency on the world coordinates $X$ and $Y$. Note that $f$ is the focal length.

motivation.text: Note that $f$ is the focal length. In many derivations, the notation is simplified by setting the focal length $f=1$. Here we will keep it to make explicit which factors depend on the camera parameters and which ones do not.

concepts.title: Properties of the Optical Flow and Parallel Motion
concepts.one_liner: Points moving parallel to the camera plane project to image motion parallel to their 3D motion, scaled inversely by distance.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how parallel 3D motion projects to image motion helps interpret optical flow patterns and depth cues.
concepts.recap_md:
- For $\dot{Z}=0$, image velocity is parallel to 3D velocity.
- Magnitude of image velocity is inversely proportional to depth $Z$.
- Optical flow reveals depth information from motion.

key_passage.text: This expression reveals a number of interesting properties of the optical flow and how it relates to motion in the world.

concepts.title: Properties of the Optical Flow and Forward Motion
concepts.one_liner: Points moving along the camera's Z axis produce image velocities proportional to their position and scaled by their relative depth change.
concepts.motivation_md: This property explains how forward or backward motion along the camera axis affects the optical flow pattern in the image.
concepts.recap_md:
- For $\dot{X} = \dot{Y} = 0$, image velocity depends on $\dot{Z}$ and position.
- Image velocity is proportional to image coordinates $(x,y)$.
- Forward motion causes radial expansion or contraction in optical flow.

concepts.title: Vanishing Point
concepts.one_liner: As time goes to infinity, the projected point converges to a vanishing point given by $\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = f \frac{V_X}{V_Z}$ and $\lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) = f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the vanishing point helps explain how points moving in 3D project onto 2D images and how their projections behave over time, especially for points moving towards or away from the camera.
concepts.recap_md:
- A 3D point moving with velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (V_X, V_Y, V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$ projects to 2D coordinates $x(t), y(t)$.
- If $V_Z \neq 0$, the 2D projection converges to a vanishing point as $t \to \infty$.
- The vanishing point coordinates are $x_\infty = f \frac{V_X}{V_Z}$ and $y_\infty = f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z}$.

concepts.title: Camera Translation Motion Field
concepts.one_liner: For a camera moving with velocity $\mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$, the 2D motion field is given by $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}-f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y  \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}V_X\\ V_Y \\ V_Z \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept models how the camera's translation causes apparent motion in the image, crucial for understanding motion fields in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera translation velocity is $\mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$.
- Scene points move relative to camera with velocity $-\mathbf{V}$.
- The 2D motion field is $\frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}-f & 0 & x \\ 0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{V}$.

key_passage.text: Let's now assume that the scene is static and that only the camera is moving. In this case, all the observed motion in the image will be due to the motion of the camera.

motivation.text: Let's now assume that the scene is static and that only the camera is moving. In this case, all the observed motion in the image will be due to the motion of the camera.

example.text:
Let's assume the camera is moving in a straight line with a velocity
$\dot{\mathbf{T}} = \mathbf{V} = (V_X,V_Y,V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$. The
translation of the camera after time $t$ will be
$\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{V} t$. A point in space
$\mathbf{P} = (X,Y,Z)^\mathsf{T}$, will move with velocity, relative to
the camera, equal to $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = -\mathbf{V}$. The moving camera
is equivalent to the case where all the scene points move relative to
the camera with the same velocity.

concepts.title: Camera Translation Motion Field Explicit Form
concepts.one_liner: The 2D motion field can be expressed explicitly as $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}V_X\\ V_Y \end{bmatrix} + \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x\\ y \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Expressing the motion field explicitly clarifies how lateral and forward components of camera velocity contribute separately to image motion.
concepts.recap_md:
- The 2D motion field splits into lateral and forward components.
- Lateral motion term: $-\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}V_X \\ V_Y \end{bmatrix}$.
- Forward motion term: $\frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$.

slots.motivation: Expressing the motion field explicitly clarifies how lateral and forward components of camera velocity contribute separately to image motion.

concepts.title: Lateral Camera Motion
concepts.one_liner: Under lateral camera motion with zero forward velocity ($V_Z=0$), the apparent velocity of a 3D point's projection is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = -\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X \\ V_Y  \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how lateral camera movement affects the apparent motion of scene points in the image, important for understanding motion parallax.
concepts.recap_md:
- Lateral camera motion means $V_Z=0$.
- The apparent image velocity is $-\frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} V_X \\ V_Y \end{bmatrix}$.
- This models motion seen through a side window of a moving car.

concepts.title: Parallax Effect in Lateral Camera Motion
concepts.one_liner: Objects close to the camera appear to move faster than distant objects under lateral camera motion, illustrating the parallax effect used to recover depth.
concepts.content:
The motion field depends on the depth at each location $Z$ as illustrated in the lateral camera translation flow figure. Objects close to the camera appear to move faster than objects farther away. Objects that are very far will appear as not moving. This parallax effect is the same one used in stereo vision to recover depth. The 2D motion in the image plane is in the opposite direction to the camera motion.

concepts.recap_md:

- Closer objects appear to move faster than distant ones.
- Far objects appear stationary, illustrating parallax used for depth recovery.

concepts.title: Camera Forward Motion and Focus of Expansion
concepts.one_liner: For forward camera motion with $V_X=V_Y=0$, the motion field is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y  \end{bmatrix}$, defining the focus of expansion.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept describes how forward camera motion causes image points to appear to expand from a focus of expansion, important for motion analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- Forward camera motion means $V_X=V_Y=0$, $V_Z \neq 0$.
- The motion field is proportional to $\frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$.
- This defines the focus of expansion in the image.

concepts.title: Time to Contact
concepts.one_liner: The observed motion depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, the inverse of the time to contact, which is the time for the camera to reach an object at distance $Z$ moving at velocity $V_Z$.
concepts.content: Equation (@eq-motion_projection_focus_expansion) provides insights: the rate of expansion does not depend on the focal length $f$, and the observed motion depends only on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact. The time to contact, $Z/V_Z$, is the time it will take the camera to reach the object located at distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$.
concepts.motivation_md: Time to contact quantifies how soon the camera will reach an object, linking image motion to real-world distances and speeds, crucial for navigation and collision avoidance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Rate of expansion is independent of focal length $f$.
- Observed motion depends on $V_Z/Z$, the inverse time to contact.
- Time to contact is the time for the camera to reach an object at distance $Z$.

concepts.title: Motion Field for Arbitrary Camera Translation
concepts.one_liner: For arbitrary camera translation, the motion field is $\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\ \dot{y}\end{bmatrix} = \frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x - x_{\infty} \\ y - y_{\infty} \end{bmatrix}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This general formula describes the image motion field for any camera translation direction, relating motion to the vanishing point and depth.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera translation velocity components $V_X, V_Y, V_Z$ are arbitrary.
- Motion field depends on $\frac{V_Z}{Z}$ and displacement from vanishing point.
- Motion field is $\frac{V_Z}{Z} \begin{bmatrix}x - x_{\infty} \\ y - y_{\infty} \end{bmatrix}$.

concepts.title: Camera Rotation Motion Model
concepts.one_liner: The camera motion field for small motions is given by $\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \mathbf{P}_t$.
concepts.content:
Let's consider a general camera motion undergoing both translation and rotation. To compute the motion field with a compact expression, we will do a number of simplifications assuming a small motion between consecutive frames. After a small time interval, $\Delta t$, the camera will move, generating a displacement in the points with respect to the camera coordinate system equal to:

$$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t}  + \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} \mathbf{P}_t
$$
where $\mathbf{T}_{\Delta t}$ is the camera translation and $\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t}$ is the camera rotation that took place over that time interval, $\Delta t$. The velocity of a 3D point with respect to the camera will be:
$$

concepts.title: Euler Angles for Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The rotation matrix can be decomposed using Euler angles (yaw, pitch, roll) as rotations along the three axes.
concepts.motivation_md: Euler angles provide a systematic way to represent 3D rotations by decomposing them into rotations about the principal axes, simplifying rotation matrix construction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Euler angles represent rotation as yaw, pitch, and roll.
- Rotation matrix is a product of three axis rotations.
- Each angle corresponds to rotation about a camera-coordinate axis.

key_passage.text: To derive the rotation, we consider the **Euler angles** and decompose the rotation using rotations along the three axes (yaw, pitch, roll): Each angle measures the rotation along the camera-coordinate axes. Using this representation of the rotation, the rotation matrix can be written as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Z & \sin \theta_Z & 0\\ -\sin \theta_Z & \cos \theta_Z & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta_Y & 0 & -\sin \theta_Y\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ \sin \theta_Y & 0 & \cos \theta_Y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \cos \theta_X & \sin \theta_X \\ 0 & -\sin \theta_X & \cos \theta_X \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} $$

concepts.title: Cross Product Matrix Form for Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The rotation-induced displacement can be expressed as a cross product matrix form: $\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_t = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t$.
concepts.content:
$$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = - \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} + (\mathbf{R}_{\Delta t} - \mathbf{I}) \mathbf{P}_t = 
- \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - 
\begin{bmatrix}
0 &  -\theta_Z & \theta_Y\\
\theta_Z & 0 &  -\theta_X \\
-\theta_Y &  \theta_X &  0 
\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf{P}_t$$ 

The last term corresponds to the cross product in matrix form (note that we changed the sign of the matrix to make the cross product form more obvious). Therefore, we can rewrite the previous expression as: 

$$\mathbf{P}_{t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{P}_{t} = 
- \mathbf{T}_{\Delta t} - \boldsymbol{\theta} \times \mathbf{P}_t
$$
